However, in Nigeria and other low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), evidence generated by NGOs, universities, and research institutions is often poorly integrated into government decision-making, resulting in delayed policy responses and inefficient resource allocation. This study proposes a context-specific AI framework to bridge this policy-data gap within Nigeria's health governance system.
Methods: This mixed-methods, phased study will develop and validate an AI-powered "Multisectoral Intelligence Hub," piloted in Zaria, Kaduna State, over six months. Stage 1 uses an NLP pipeline built on the OpenAI GPT API to scan, extract, and summarize health reports, outbreak alerts, and policy briefs from 8-10 verified sources, including NCDC situation reports, Kaduna State Ministry of Health bulletins, Ahmadu Bello University research repositories, WHO AFRO outbreak news, Africa CDC bulletins, and AJOL-indexed journals. Extraction accuracy will be validated against 100 manually annotated documents using precision, recall, and F1-score. Stage 2 scores extracted recommendations using a composite urgency-relevance index built from five weighted variables: event severity, population vulnerability, geographic relevance, topic-ministry alignment, and source credibility, with weights set via a Delphi exercise involving 8 to 10 experts. Recommendations exceeding threshold scores are routed through a dashboard, automated email digest, and SMS alerts for high-urgency items. Stage 3 involves stakeholder validation with 15 ministry officials and 10 civil society/NGO representatives via semi-structured interviews and an adapted System Usability Scale survey, analyzed thematically and descriptively. The framework incorporates a data provenance/verification layer and human-in-the-loop review before dissemination, follows informed consent and anonymization procedures, and will seek approval from the ABUTH Health Research Ethics Committee in compliance with the Nigeria Data Protection Act. Performance will be evaluated using NLP accuracy, response time reduction, policy uptake rate, and stakeholder satisfaction.
Expected Outcomes: The framework is expected to reduce bureaucratic delays, improve real-time situational awareness, and accelerate evidence-based decision-making, while strengthening multisectoral collaboration, resource allocation, and emergency response capacity.
Conclusion: Strong data-driven frameworks are essential for sustainable health systems. This pilot offers a potentially scalable and replicable model for addressing the policy-data gap in Nigeria and similar LMIC contexts.

title: TinyMed-NG: Fully Offline Multilingual Medical AI for Nigerian Rural Health Workers, Deployed on Commodity Android Devices
abstract:
Background: Community Health Extension Workers form the frontline of rural healthcare delivery across Nigeria, yet frequently operate without specialist consultation, reference materials in local languages, or reliable internet connectivity. Existing medical language models are cloud-dependent and English-centric, making them unusable in the settings where frontline health workers most need decision support. Methods: We developed TinyMed-NG, a fully offline multilingual medical language model system built on Llama 3.2 3B Instruct. The model was fine-tuned in two stages: supervised fine-tuning via QLoRA on 3,917 curated medical question-answer pairs spanning Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, and Nigerian Pidgin English, covering malaria, typhoid, maternal health, child health, wound management, and emergency recognition; followed by Direct Preference Optimization using synthetic preference pairs to improve language adherence and reduce code-switching. The model was quantized to Q2_K format (1.36 GB, a 4.7x compression from the merged 16-bit model) and deployed via llama.cpp on Android ARM64 devices with no internet connectivity, including an integrated on-device Electronic Medical Record module and a multilingual emergency referral alerting system.
Results: SFT training achieved a final cross-entropy loss of 1.099 over 932 steps. DPO training yielded a chosen response reward of 28.86 versus a rejected response reward of 10.46, a margin of 18.40, with 0.95 reward accuracy, confirming successful preference alignment across all four languages. The deployed system runs on a TECNO CAMON 40 Pro (8GB RAM) with average on-device inference latency of 62 seconds and a minimum requirement of 2GB available RAM, matching the typical constraint of rural-deployed Android devices in Nigerian markets. We additionally identified and resolved a previously undocumented Llama 3 GGUF tokenizer incompatibility affecting standard llama.cpp Android deployments, a fix required for any Llama 3 model deployed offline on Android via this widely used runtime.
Conclusion: TinyMed-NG demonstrates that fully offline, multilingual, safety-conscious medical AI is achievable on commodity Android hardware already in the hands of Nigerian rural health workers, without dependence on connectivity or cloud infrastructure. This offers a practical, country-led path to extending AI-enabled clinical decision support into the lowest-connectivity, highest-need settings across the continent.

title: Creating an Ethics Toolkit for the Development and Deployment of AI Healthcare Tools in Sub-Saharan Africa.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare delivery worldwide, with applications ranging from diagnostic imaging to clinical decision support and disease surveillance. While AI holds transformative potential for addressing healthcare challenges in resource-constrained settings, its proliferation in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has largely proceeded without context-appropriate ethical frameworks to guide its development and deployment. Sub-Saharan Africa faces a unique confluence of healthcare challenges that both amplify AI's potential benefits and heighten risks of harm.
OBJECTIVES: This research aims to develop, validate, and refine a practical ethics toolkit for healthcare AI implementation specifically tailored to Sub-Saharan African contexts. It will answer the question: How can ethical principles for AI in healthcare be translated into a practical, context-appropriate toolkit that guides stakeholders through ethical considerations during the development, procurement, deployment, and governance of AI healthcare tools in SSA settings?
METHODS: This study will use a mixed-methods design and proceed in three sequential phases: scoping review of existing literature, toolkit development, and expert validation via the modified Delphi method. The study population will primarily be healthcare stakeholders in sub-Saharan Africa, including but not limited to developers, implementers, clinicians, patients, families and community members.
RESULTS: This study will produce a handy and practical ethics toolkit for the equitable development, deployment and governance of healthcare AI in Sub-Saharan Africa.
CONCLUSION: AI has brought immense benefits to the healthcare sector. However, its integration does not go without consideration, ethically and legally. This research addresses the urgent need for practical, implementable tools that can guide more equitable AI healthcare implementation, producing a resource with immediate real-world applicability while serving as a foundation for future empirical research on ethical AI healthcare governance in diverse global contexts.

title: Preparing Future Healthcare Professionals for AI-Driven Healthcare: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Undergraduate Health Professions Education
abstract:
Background: There is a critical lack of preparedness among undergraduate education programmes of the health professions to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare delivery. Findings also show that students' AI knowledge is generally low. Most students got the knowledge through social media, and not from curriculum as evidenced by the various studies conducted across the globe. This review aims to explore the current state of AI in undergraduate health professional education across the world and in low-resource settings.
Objectives: To assess existing roles and responsibilities of AI in healthcare, identify the competencies that are needed in AI literacy, assess strategies for implementing AI literacy in curricula, and explore barriers and opportunities for implementation.
Methods: The structured narrative review was performed on PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, ERIC, Scopus, The Web of Science and Google Scholar using a Boolean Search to find articles that discussed AI technologies, competency outcome terms, and health professions education. Peer-reviewed articles and policy documents from 2022 to 2026 that focused on undergraduate health professional students, and available in full text in English, were included. Those studies that were conducted at the post-graduate level and engineering papers in the field of AI (not health education literature) were not included.
Results: The five AI literacy competency domains identified were: foundational knowledge, critical evaluation, clinical application, data governance, and ethical reasoning. Here are a few best practices for these methods: simulation learning, generative AI tools, and interdisciplinary training. Some of the challenges include: faculty inadequacies, curriculum overload, lack of accreditation requirements, and resource disparities among Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMIC).
Conclusion: Systematic incorporation of competency-based AI literacy is needed throughout all undergraduate health professional programs. Clinically contextualised teaching, teacher training and equipping with a strategy that prioritises equity are essential for sustainable reform of AI teaching so that future health professionals will be able to safely use AI technologies without sacrificing humanistic care.

title: Reducing Medicines Regulatory Approval Timelines in Africa Through an AI-Enabled Compliance Platform, A Multi-Country Implementation Experience Across 10 African Markets
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In much of Africa, the barrier to essential medicines is not that the drugs don't exist it's the paperwork standing between them and patients. Fifty-four national regulators each set their own requirements, formats and working languages, and a single product registration takes roughly 18 months per country. Companies spend an estimated USD 2-5 million per product on compliance before any medicine is sold, a cost that quietly shuts out local and mid-sized manufacturers and narrows what reaches pharmacy shelves. With the African Medicines Agency and AfCFTA now pushing toward harmonisation, we set out to test whether AI tooling could shorten those timelines in practice, not just in principle.
METHODS: We built and deployed AIcyclinder, a cloud platform that applies natural language processing and machine learning across the regulatory lifecycle. It does five things: assembles Common Technical Document dossiers and scores them for completeness against each authority's specific rules; translates and adapts documents across English, French, Portuguese and Kiswahili; tracks rule changes across all 54 regulators; scans Africa-specific pharmaceutical literature and flags safety signals; and automates adverse event reporting end to end. The platform has run commercially since 2023 with manufacturers and distributors across East and Southern Africa. We report what we observed in routine use dossiers handled, countries covered, submission completeness and how long preparation actually took.
RESULT: From 2023 to 2025 the platform processed more than 100 dossiers across 10 countries, for clients ranging from multinational generics manufacturers to national producers and regional distributors. Automated assembly and pre-submission scoring brought preparation down from the 18-month baseline to a matter of weeks. Users reported markedly fewer document errors and rejections, which they attributed to the gap analysis catching omissions before submission and to consistent language adaptation. Automated pharmacovigilance cut the manual burden of adverse event reporting. Medicines whose submissions passed through the platform reach an estimated 100 million patients through client products, and adoption grew steadily throughout, with usage and recurring revenue doubling each year.
CONCLUSION: Africa-specific AI tooling, built locally, can meaningfully shorten regulatory timelines and lower the cost of compliance and both translate directly into faster patient access. The cost reduction matters most for local manufacturers, who stand to gain markets that were previously priced out of reach. These findings come with real limits: we had no control group, the data is operational rather than trial-derived, and performance varies between authorities. The work ahead is formal evaluation against matched comparators, direct engagement with national regulators on interoperability, and alignment with continental harmonisation so that AI regulatory infrastructure is built once, as shared public good, rather than fragmented across competing vendors.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Toward Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Among Pharmacy Students in Malawi and Guinea: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare through applications in clinical decision support, drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, personalized medicine, and pharmaceutical care. As future healthcare professionals, pharmacy students must acquire adequate AI competencies to effectively integrate these technologies into practice. Despite the increasing use of AI tools by students, formal AI education remains limited in many African pharmacy schools. Evidence on pharmacy students' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding AI is scarce, and no comparative study has previously been conducted between Guinea and Malawi. This study aimed to assess AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices among pharmacy students in both countries and identify factors associated with AI use.
Methods: A multicenter analytical cross-sectional study was conducted over six months among pharmacy students enrolled at the Faculty of Pharmacy, Universite Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry (Guinea) and the Bachelor of Pharmacy Programme, Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (Malawi) during the 2025-2026 academic year. An exhaustive online survey was administered using KoboToolbox to all eligible students who provided informed consent. The questionnaire consisted of five sections covering sociodemographic characteristics, AI exposure, knowledge, attitudes, and practices. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants' characteristics. Bivariate associations were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test, followed by multivariable logistic regression to identify factors independently associated with good AI practices. Statistical significance was set at p less than 0.05.
Results: A total of 322 pharmacy students participated, including 167 males (51.9%) and 155 females (48.1%), with a mean age of 24.0 plus/minus 4.2 years. Of the participants, 115 (35.7%) were from Guinea and 207 (64.3%) from Malawi. Overall, 44.7% demonstrated poor AI knowledge, whereas only 13.0% achieved good knowledge. Attitudes toward AI were predominantly neutral (61.9%), with 30.2% reporting positive attitudes and 7.9% reporting negative attitudes. Regarding AI practices, 35.7% exhibited poor practices, 44.7% moderate practices, and only 19.6% demonstrated good practices. Bivariate analysis showed that the country of study was significantly associated with knowledge (p = 0.002), attitudes (p less than 0.001), and practices (p = 0.004). Age was significantly associated with AI practices (p = 0.020), whereas sex and academic level were not significantly associated. Multivariable logistic regression confirmed that the country of study remained an independent predictor of good AI practices after adjustment for potential confounders.
Conclusion: Pharmacy students in Guinea and Malawi demonstrated inadequate knowledge and limited use of AI despite generally positive or neutral attitudes toward these technologies. These findings reveal important gaps in AI preparedness among future pharmacists and emphasize the urgent need to integrate structured AI education into undergraduate pharmacy curricula across Africa. Strengthening AI competencies through curriculum reform, practical training, and responsible AI implementation will better equip future pharmacists to leverage AI for improved pharmaceutical care, clinical decision-making, and healthcare innovation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Balancing Innovation, Patient Rights, and Legal Governance in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing healthcare by improving diagnostic accuracy, facilitating precision medicine, enhancing disease surveillance, streamlining administrative processes, and expanding access to healthcare through telemedicine and intelligent clinical decision-support systems. As healthcare systems increasingly embrace AI-driven technologies, significant questions arise concerning patient safety, data protection, accountability, professional liability, informed consent, and the protection of fundamental human rights. These concerns are particularly pronounced in developing countries such as Nigeria, where the legal and regulatory framework governing AI in healthcare remains in its infancy despite the growing adoption of digital health technologies.
METHOD: This paper critically examines the legal and ethical implications of integrating AI into Nigeria's healthcare system. It evaluates the adequacy of existing legal instruments governing health information, patient privacy, professional responsibility, and digital innovation in addressing emerging challenges associated with AI-assisted healthcare. The paper further explores issues of algorithmic bias, transparency, explainability, cybersecurity, cross-border data governance, and equitable access to AI-powered healthcare, with particular attention to their implications for vulnerable populations.
RESULTS: Drawing on comparative international practices and emerging global AI governance principles, the paper identifies regulatory gaps within the Nigerian healthcare landscape and proposes a framework for responsible AI governance that promotes innovation while safeguarding patient rights and public confidence. It argues that an effective governance model should incorporate robust data protection standards, ethical oversight, clear liability regimes, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continuous regulatory adaptation to technological developments.
CONCLUSION: The paper concludes that although Artificial Intelligence possesses immense potential to improve healthcare delivery and strengthen Nigeria's health system, its sustainable adoption depends upon a legal framework that balances innovation with accountability, transparency, equity, and respect for human dignity. It recommends legislative reforms, institutional capacity building, and the development of national AI governance guidelines tailored to Nigeria's healthcare ecosystem to ensure that AI remains a tool for advancing public health rather than creating new forms of inequality or legal uncertainty.

title: Toward equitable digital health: an integrated framework addressing exclusion, ethics, and implementation across healthcare systems
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Digital health technologies are fundamentally reshaping healthcare delivery, access, and governance worldwide. While these innovations offer unprecedented opportunities to extend services, particularly in resource-constrained settings, early implementation experiences from large-scale platforms such as India's Co-WIN vaccination system and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) reveal that poorly designed digitalization can entrench or even widen existing health inequities. Despite growing recognition of these challenges, there remains an urgent need for a coherent analytical framework to understand how patterns of digital exclusion, ethical challenges, and implementation barriers interact to shape digital health outcomes across diverse healthcare systems. Objectives This narrative review aims to: (1) synthesize current evidence on patterns and mechanisms of digital health exclusion across socioeconomic, geographic, and demographic dimensions; (2) identify key ethical and governance challenges, including informed consent, data protection, algorithmic fairness, and cybersecurity, in contemporary digital health implementations; (3) analyze implementation experiences from India and comparable low- and middle-income country (LMIC) settings; and (4) propose an integrated equity framework to guide more inclusive digital health strategies that can inform policy, practice, and future research.
CONCLUSION: Digital health will not inherently advance health equity; rather, equity must be intentionally designed, systematically governed, and continuously monitored throughout the implementation lifecycle. We propose an integrated Digital Health Equity Framework that explicitly links patterns of exclusion with ethical safeguards and implementation strategies. Core components include: participatory co-design with marginalized communities, privacy-by-design and safety-by-design architectures, multi-channel service delivery that preserves non-digital pathways, routine disaggregated equity monitoring, and transparent algorithmic governance with redress mechanisms. Application of this framework can help policymakers, health system leaders, and technology developers ensure that national digital health programs, in India and globally, close rather than widen equity gaps, ultimately advancing universal health coverage through inclusive digital transformation.

title: Governance by Design Transfer Pilot for Accountable Digital Hospital Pathways in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hospitals in resource-constrained settings often face fragmented governance, weak pathway accountability, uneven digital maturity, and limited visibility over safety, resource use, workforce participation, and patient-centred outcomes. These challenges are especially harmful for low-income patients, who are more likely to experience delays, repeat visits, poor handoffs, avoidable costs, and discontinuity of care. Governance by Design was developed from empirical PhD research in a Malaysian teaching hospital, where Process Orientation was shown to improve patient-centred performance through key internal mediators, especially patient safety, financial stewardship, and workforce engagement. This abstract presents an adapted Nigerian transfer pilot designed to test whether the Governance by Design model can be operationalised in a different health-system context.
METHODS: The proposed pilot will adapt a preregistered pathway-centred governance architecture to selected Nigerian hospital pathways. The model assigns named pathway owners, codifies decision rights, establishes pathway boards, standardises high-risk handoff audits, tracks incident-learning closure, monitors workforce participation, and links stewardship indicators to pathway dashboards. The pilot will first assess available hard-copy and digital records, including incident logs, handoff records, finance/stewardship records, staff participation records, operational registers, and existing HIS/EMR/EHR data where available. Where baseline data are missing, the project will prospectively generate them through structured pathway registers, audit forms, incident-learning logs, stewardship templates, participation records, and minimum viable dashboards. Evaluation will assess governance fidelity, data readiness, dashboard usability, baseline KPI generation, and readiness for stronger quasi-experimental analysis, including interrupted time series or staged pathway comparison where feasible.
EXPECTED RESULTS: The pilot is expected to produce a transferable governance technology package consisting of pathway-owner templates, decision-rights charters, KPI dictionaries, dashboard fields, data-quality gates, incident-learning SLA logs, handoff audit tools, stewardship trackers, and fidelity-audit routines. Expected early outcomes include improved visibility of patient safety processes, stronger governance participation, more structured resource tracking, and better readiness for later quasi-experimental evaluation.
CONCLUSION: Governance by Design offers a scalable, AI- and data-ready governance architecture for improving hospital accountability before full digital maturity is achieved. Its transferability lies in its ability to work with paper records, spreadsheets, simple dashboards, or future HIS/EMR/EHR integration. The Nigerian pilot can generate practical evidence for country-led AI-enabled health governance, digital accountability, and patient-centred health-system strengthening.

title: Development and Integration of an AI-Enabled Preeclampsia Risk Stratification and Pregnancy Outcomes Registry into Hospital Electronic Medical Records in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia and other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are among the leading direct causes of maternal death worldwide, accounting for approximately 16% of the 287,000 maternal deaths recorded globally in 2020, and an estimated 50,000 deaths, per the World Health Organization's most recent analysis of maternal mortality causes. The condition affects 3-8% of pregnancies worldwide, with its burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa. Nigeria illustrates this starkly with National maternal mortality estimated at 993 per 100,000 live births, rising above 1,000 per 100,000 in several Northern States. A recent meta-analysis of Nigerian pregnancy cohorts reported a pooled preeclampsia/eclampsia prevalence of 4.51%, an associated maternal mortality rate of 6.04%, and a fetal mortality rate of 16.73%. This burden is large, geographically concentrated, and substantially preventable through timely risk identification and low-cost prophylaxis, making the absence of a locally deployable screening tool an urgent gap rather than a theoretical one. Yet the risk-prediction models with the strongest evidence base were validated in settings with routine biomarker and Doppler access that many Nigerian antenatal facilities lack, leaving providers without an auditable, locally appropriate tool for early risk stratification.
METHODS: Preeclampsia Prediction Prevention and Surveillance (PREPPS) combines two risk-stratification pathways: a Tier 1 competing-risks model using maternal history, mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (Ut A PI), and angiogenic biomarkers where available, and a Tier 2 calibrated gradient-boosted model using history and MAP, or history and Ut A PI alone, where they are not, so facilities lacking biomarker access remain served rather than excluded. Both pathways operate alongside a deterministic safety-rule layer flagging severe presentations irrespective of model output, with per-patient explanations via SHAP or an Explainable Boosting Machine. Integration is achieved through an EMR-agnostic HL7 FHIR interface, and a longitudinal outcomes registry links each classification to eventual delivery and neonatal outcomes; overrides are logged with a mandatory rationale, governed by Nigeria Data Protection Act compliance and Health Research Ethics Committee oversight.
RESULTS: The system architecture, tiered modelling specification, and antenatal data schema are finalised, and algorithm adaptation for the Nigerian clinical context is complete. An EMR-integrated PREPPS pilot module using the FHIR interface has been built for deployment at National Hospital Abuja, the designated single-site pilot facility, where Health Research Ethics Committee review is underway alongside finalisation of the pilot design and the developer-facility data sharing agreement. The validation plan specifies concrete next steps viz: prospective single-centre validation with refinement of decision-support prompts and registry fields; multi-centre expansion across tertiary and selected secondary facilities for external validation and recalibration; and integration with Ministry of Health maternal health information systems to support national scale-up and dissemination of registry-derived outcomes data. Clinical performance results are not yet available.
CONCLUSION: PREPPS closes the gap between validated preeclampsia risk models and Nigeria's deployable infrastructure with a completed system design, an adapted algorithm, and an EMR-integrated pilot ready for deployment at National Hospital Abuja.

title: The state of the data ecosystem in health facilities in Uganda: A multi-center study with application on stroke data
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Stroke is an increasing public health challenge in low- and middle-income countries, yet the availability, quality, and usability of stroke data systems required to support surveillance, clinical care, research, and policy remain poorly characterized. Understanding the existing stroke data ecosystem is essential for identifying opportunities to strengthen data-driven stroke care and health system planning. This study assessed the structure and functionality of the stroke data ecosystem across selected hospitals in Uganda.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional multi-center descriptive study among six tertiary health facilities providing stroke care in Uganda. Data were collected from April to June 2026 using a structured assessment tool covering four domains of the stroke data ecosystem: data governance, data architecture and management, digital platforms and infrastructure, and data users and utilization. Information was collected from facility representatives responsible for stroke data management, primarily medical records officers. Descriptive analyses were conducted to summarize the availability of data systems, governance practices, infrastructure, workforce capacity, and use of stroke information for clinical care, reporting, research, and decision-making.
RESULTS: Five tertiary-level referral hospitals and one secondary-level specialized facility participated in this study. All facilities maintained stroke registries and provided rehabilitation services, while five provided acute stroke care and neuroimaging services. Four hospitals used electronic stroke registries, whereas two relied on paper-based systems. Foundational governance structures were commonly reported, with most facilities having data governance frameworks (4/6), dedicated leadership, accountability mechanisms, and routine reporting processes. However, formal governance structures such as steering committees and advanced data-sharing mechanisms were less consistently implemented. All hospitals used standardized stroke definitions and diagnostic coding systems, and most (4/6) maintained metadata documentation and conducted routine data quality checks. However, longitudinal data capture remained limited, with post-discharge follow-up information collected in only two facilities. Digital infrastructure was widely available, including local servers, cloud-based storage, user authentication, and routine submission of stroke data to the national DHIS2 platform. However, information technology support and integration of advanced analytics varied across facilities. Stroke data were routinely used for clinical care, hospital reporting, planning, and research, although the availability of specialized analytical skills and advanced data products differed between institutions.
CONCLUSION: Health facilities in Uganda have established important components of a stroke data ecosystem, however, gaps remain in longitudinal patient tracking, advanced analytics, interoperability, and specialized workforce capacity. Strengthening these areas will be critical for developing integrated stroke information systems capable of supporting clinical decision-making, research, surveillance, and policy development.

title: DATA HEALTH SYSTEM: An Integrated Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence Platform for Strengthening Health Systems and Data-Driven Decision-Making in Chad
abstract:
Background: Health systems in many low-resource settings face significant challenges related to fragmented health data, limited interoperability between information systems, delayed reporting, inefficient resource management, and insufficient use of data for evidence-based decision-making. In Chad, these constraints particularly affect the quality of healthcare services, maternal, newborn, and reproductive health outcomes, pharmaceutical supply management, disease surveillance, and overall health system coordination. To address these challenges, DATA HEALTH SYSTEM was conceived as an integrated digital health platform combining interoperability, secure health data management, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities to support healthcare delivery and health system strengthening.
Methods: DATA HEALTH SYSTEM is currently under development as a proof-of-concept prototype. The platform adopts a modular architecture integrating key healthcare components, including Electronic Medical Records (EMR), Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH), Maternal and Child Health services, Laboratory Information Management, Medical Imaging, Blood Bank Management, Pharmacy and Supply Chain Management, Human Resource Management, Hospital Administration, Telemedicine, Referral and Counter-Referral Systems, and real-time decision-support dashboards. The technical architecture is designed around internationally recognized interoperability standards, including HL7 FHIR, OpenHIE, DICOM, and secure APIs, enabling integration with national health information systems such as DHIS2 and electronic Logistics Management Information Systems (eLMIS). The platform incorporates robust security mechanisms, including data encryption, multi-factor authentication, role-based access control (RBAC), and audit logging. AI functionalities currently under development aim to support early identification of high-risk pregnancies, predictive analysis of medicine stock-outs, public health surveillance, and clinical decision support.
Results: The prototype demonstrates the technical feasibility of an integrated digital health ecosystem capable of consolidating clinical, logistical, and administrative health data within a unified platform. The proposed architecture enables secure data exchange across healthcare facilities and national health information systems while supporting real-time access to health information. The prototype shows the potential to improve continuity of care, strengthen reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health services, enhance supply chain visibility, and improve data quality for operational and strategic decision-making. AI-enabled modules under development are expected to transform routine health data into actionable insights for healthcare providers, health managers, and policymakers.
Conclusion: DATA HEALTH SYSTEM represents a locally driven digital health innovation aligned with the World Health Organization's Global Strategy on Digital Health and international interoperability principles. By integrating digital health technologies, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and health data governance within a single platform, the system has the potential to strengthen healthcare delivery, improve operational efficiency, and support data-driven decision-making in resource-constrained settings. Future work will focus on full platform development, pilot implementation in selected healthcare facilities, and evaluation of its impact on healthcare quality, health system performance, and public health outcomes.

title: Integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation into the ECEWS Central Data Repository for Intelligent Analysis of Longitudinal Electronic Health Records
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Electronic health records contain extensive longitudinal information that can support patient management, programme monitoring, data-quality improvement, and public health decision-making. However, retrieving and reviewing patient-level information across clinical encounters, pharmacy records, laboratory investigations, treatment outcomes, and demographic records is often time-consuming and may require specialised database or analytical skills. Excellence Community Education Welfare Scheme, ECEWS, therefore developed and integrated a Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG, solution into its Central Data Repository to enable authorised users to retrieve and interpret electronic health record information through a conversational interface.
METHODS: The solution combines a secure information-retrieval architecture, a large language model, and the existing ECEWS Central Data Repository. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data from ECEWS-supported health facilities in Delta, Ekiti, and Osun States were processed and made available through a controlled retrieval layer. The system provides a chat-based interface through which authorised users can submit natural-language questions about patient records. In response to each query, the system searches the Central Data Repository, retrieves the most relevant patient-level information, and generates a structured response grounded in the available source records. The solution was designed to retrieve and present demographic information, clinical encounter histories, antiretroviral treatment records, medication histories, laboratory results, appointment histories, treatment outcomes, biometric information, and other available longitudinal patient data. It also supports the visual presentation of selected patient information through charts and summarised historical timelines. Role-based access controls, audit logging, data de-identification, source referencing, and response-validation mechanisms were incorporated to protect patient confidentiality and reduce the risk of unsupported model-generated responses.
RESULTS: The RAG solution was successfully integrated into the ECEWS Central Data Repository and deployed as a conversational interface for retrieving longitudinal patient information. The system enables authorised users to enter natural-language questions and receive consolidated responses drawn from historical electronic health records across ECEWS-supported facilities in Delta, Ekiti, and Osun States. Through the chat interface, users can retrieve patient demographic information, clinical visit histories, medication and antiretroviral therapy records, laboratory results, appointment records, treatment outcomes, biometric information, and other historical data available within the repository. The system can also organise retrieved information into chronological patient summaries, historical timelines, tables, and charts, making it easier to understand changes in a patient's clinical and treatment history over time. The solution reduces the need for users to search through multiple electronic forms, dashboards, database tables, and individual patient records. It also provides an alternative to depending exclusively on manually written database queries or predefined reports. Retrieved responses remain linked to the underlying source data, allowing health information, clinical, and programme teams to verify the information presented by the system. Initial implementation demonstrated the feasibility of using RAG to support rapid patient-history retrieval, longitudinal record review, identification of documentation gaps, review of treatment and laboratory histories, and exploration of patient and programme-level patterns. Formal evaluation is ongoing to quantify the system's accuracy, retrieval time, usability, completeness, and potential reduction in manual patient-record review time.
Conclusion: The integration of Retrieval-Augmented Generation into the ECEWS Central Data Repository demonstrates a practical application of generative artificial intelligence for retrieving and interpreting longitudinal electronic health records in a public health programme. By providing a secure conversational interface, the solution enables authorised users to access patient demographic, clinical, laboratory, medication, and treatment-history information in a more accessible and organised format. The system has the potential to improve the efficiency of patient-record review, clinical follow-up, data-quality assurance, programme monitoring, and evidence-based decision-making. Further evaluation will establish its accuracy, performance, user acceptability, and measurable effect on routine health information and programme-management processes.

title: Using Large Language Models to Improve the Quality and Consistency of Community Health Programme Field Reports in Resource Constrained Settings: An Early Implementation Experience from Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Community health and development programmes rely heavily on narrative field reports to monitor implementation, document community engagement activities, and support decision-making. However, reports prepared by field officers frequently contain English language errors, incomplete information, inconsistencies, and poor structure, thereby requiring significant supervisory review before they can be used for programme management or donor reporting. While artificial intelligence has received considerable attention for clinical applications, its potential to improve operational reporting within health programmes remains underexplored.
METHODS: Sendiflow is an AI-assisted reporting platform developed to improve the quality, consistency, and completeness of field reports submitted by programme personnel. The platform combines structured data capture with large language model capabilities to enhance technical writing, identify inconsistencies, prompt users to address missing information, and standardize report presentation before supervisor review. The solution was designed based on extensive experience supporting monitoring, evaluation, communication, and reporting processes across health and development programmes.
RESULTS: Early implementation demonstrates the feasibility of integrating large language models into routine programme reporting workflows. Initial testing indicates that the platform can improve report clarity, strengthen consistency between structured data and narrative descriptions, and reduce the amount of manual editing required prior to supervisory review. Formal evaluation of reporting quality, user satisfaction, and workflow efficiency is planned as implementation expands across additional organizations. We already have one client, Lawyers Alert (a regional NGO) actively using the tool with very good reviews.
CONCLUSION: Artificial intelligence has significant potential beyond clinical decision support. AI-assisted reporting platforms may strengthen programme implementation by improving documentation quality, supporting more consistent monitoring and evaluation practices, and reducing administrative burden within resource-constrained health systems. Further implementation research is warranted to evaluate long-term impact on reporting quality, programme management, and organizational efficiency.

title: Building AI-Ready HIV Data Systems Through Automated EMR Data Quality Review: Experience from QCheck in Niger State
abstract:
Background: Good HIV program reporting depends on the quality of documentation done at facility level. In Niger State, routine review of retention and audit determination tool (RADET) and electronic medical record (EMR) exports showed recurring gaps in client records, including incomplete tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT) documentation, missing pharmacy pickup information, viral load-related errors, enhanced adherence counselling (EAC) gaps, duplicate identifiers, and inconsistent antiretroviral therapy (ART) dates. Reviewing these gaps manually across many facilities required repeated Excel analysis, technical support, and considerable staff time. QCheck was introduced as a locally developed offline tool to run automated rule-based checks on routine EMR/RADET exports and help teams quickly identify records needing correction or follow-up.
Objective: To assess how QCheck supported routine HIV data quality review across 37 health facilities in Niger State, Nigeria, and contributed to more complete and usable datasets for future AI-enabled HIV program monitoring.
Methods: Routine HIV EMR/RADET data from 37 facilities were reviewed from October 2025 to June 2026. The review covered 47,825 client records, including 25,474 active clients. Data entry clerks and program staff used QCheck to check 24 indicators covering TPT documentation, viral load monitoring, EAC commencement, pharmacy pickup, ART status, CD4 documentation, and duplicate identifiers. The tool produced facility summaries and client-level line lists, which were shared with facility teams for verification, correction, and follow-up. Initial and endline gap counts were compared. Counts represented total gap occurrences across the 24 indicators, meaning one client could contribute to more than one gap.
Results: Across the 24 indicators, documented gaps reduced from 11,201 to 3,829, representing a 65.8% reduction. Several gaps were fully resolved, including absent CD4 results, CD4 documentation issues among children younger than 5 years, blank care entry point, ART/enrollment date-sequencing errors, and TB-negative TX_NEW clients incorrectly started on TB treatment. Notable reductions were also seen in TPT initiation without completion date or status (2,022 to 167), TX_NEW clients eligible for but not initiated on TPT (1,287 to 129), missed TPT opportunities (726 to 69), missing last pickup date (213 to 9), incorrect regimen (80 to 3), and unsuppressed clients without EAC commencement (541 to 181). Gaps still common by June 2026 included CD4 less than 200 without TB-LAM testing, duplicate unique identifiers, invalid CD4 results, and incomplete EAC documentation.
Conclusion: QCheck helped facility and program teams move from broad manual review to focused client-level action. By showing where gaps were occurring and which clients or facilities needed attention, the tool supported routine correction of documentation and service delivery gaps. The reduction seen during the review period suggests that locally developed offline data quality tools can strengthen routine data use and program monitoring in resource-limited settings. Cleaner and more consistent EMR data also provide a practical foundation for responsible, AI-ready HIV data systems.

title: Is Your Data Ready for AI Adoption? A Practical Maturity Framework for Health Data Pipelines in Africa
abstract:
Background: AI-in-health strategies across Africa frequently begin at the model layer, selecting algorithms and piloting use cases, while underestimating whether the underlying data pipeline can sustain them. Health data across the continent is often disjointed across paper records, standalone electronic health record systems, laboratory systems, insurance databases, and mobile health applications that cannot connect with each other, producing chronic problems in completeness, duplication, timeliness, and semantic consistency. Recent analysis frames Africa's constraint as distinct from high-income settings. The binding issues are fragmented data ecosystems, unreliable infrastructure, and thin institutional capacity to govern digital technologies, rather than a shortage of AI ambition.
Methods: This work proposes a five-stage data pipeline readiness framework: Fragmented, Collected, Structured, Governed, and AI-Ready. It was developed through hands-on experience building and auditing health data pipelines with SQL, Python, Looker Studio, and Power BI and informed by the broader maturity-model literature, including recent systematic reviews synthesising dozens of healthcare AI governance and information-system maturity models, most grounded in Capability Maturity Model Integration principles adapted to healthcare. Each stage is assessed across five dimensions: collection consistency, standardisation and coding, governance and access control, cross-source integration, and analytics tooling maturity. The framework is designed for practical diagnostic use rather than as a purely conceptual model.
Results: Applied to a composite scenario modelled on documented patterns across the continent, a national health program pursuing predictive analytics reflects a common finding in the literature. AI pilots frequently integrate only with a single vertical program's database, such as an HIV or TB system, because the national EHR platform lacks interoperable architecture, which prevents the pilot from expanding to other departments or regions. This composite program sits at the "collected" stage: data exists, but inconsistent coding and absent governance block integration with the wider health system. This echoes federated efforts elsewhere that report unreliable connectivity, low digital health literacy, and institutional reluctance to share data as persistent structural barriers. By contrast, harmonisation initiatives such as the pan-African INSPIRE datahub, which applies a common data model to integrate longitudinal population health data across multiple African studies, illustrate what progress toward the "Structured/Governed" stage looks like in practice.
Conclusion: A practical, non-technical readiness framework gives African health system leaders, NGOs, and startups a shared diagnostic language for assessing AI-readiness before committing to AI-specific investment. By foregrounding pipeline maturity, meaning collection, standardisation, governance, and integration, as a prerequisite rather than an afterthought, this approach supports more realistic AI adoption planning. It directly addresses Track C2's focus on the data infrastructure needed to power scalable, sustainable health AI across the continent.

title: Building an AI-Ready Neuromodulation Data Infrastructure for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Outcomes in West Africa
abstract:
Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is an emerging intervention for treatment-resistant depression and other neuropsychiatric conditions. However, structured real-world TMS outcome data from African populations remains scarce. This limits local clinical benchmarking, protocol optimization, AI model development, and health-system planning for mental health care.
Methods: A prospective data infrastructure will be implemented within a TMS clinical setting in Lagos, Nigeria. Data will be captured at baseline intake, treatment sessions, interim reviews, and post-treatment follow-up. Variables will include demographics, clinical history, symptom severity, stimulation parameters, adherence, adverse events, and standardized outcome scores. A tiered consent process will distinguish clinical-use data from anonymized research-use data. Records will undergo de-identification, anonymization, and minimum cohort-size safeguards before storage in a secure research warehouse. Engineered features will measure response, remission, adherence, protocol variation, and longitudinal symptom change. Once sufficient completed treatment courses are available, predictive models will be trained to identify factors associated with treatment response and support protocol recommendation.
Results: The project is expected to generate one of the first structured, AI-ready TMS outcome datasets for an African population. Anticipated outputs include longitudinal treatment response profiles, real-world adherence and safety indicators, benchmarking reports, and preliminary predictive models for TMS response. These outputs will support clinical audit, evidence generation, and future decision-support tools tailored to local patient characteristics.
Conclusions: Structured neuromodulation data infrastructure can transform routine TMS care into ethically governed real-world evidence. By enabling anonymized analysis, benchmarking, and predictive modeling, this initiative provides a foundation for locally relevant AI in mental health and may improve the personalization and scalability of TMS services in low-data health systems.

title: From Fragmented Hospital Records to an AI-Ready Data Ecosystem: Implementing the OMOP Common Data Model at Douala General Hospital, Cameroon
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence in health cannot be developed or scaled responsibly without interoperable, high-quality, and locally governed clinical data. At Douala General Hospital in Cameroon, routine health information was distributed across paper records, spreadsheets, programme-specific databases, and an HIV electronic medical record. Differences in data structures, clinical terminology, completeness, and documentation limited cross-programme analyses and the reuse of data for artificial intelligence and advanced analytics. This project aimed to establish a locally led and reusable pipeline for transforming heterogeneous hospital records into an interoperable and AI-ready clinical data ecosystem using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model.
METHODS: A phased extract-transform-load implementation was conducted across three priority clinical domains: respiratory diseases, tuberculosis, and HIV. Source databases were profiled using WhiteRabbit, source-to-target specifications were developed with Rabbit-in-a-Hat, and local clinical terms were mapped to standard concepts using Usagi and OHDSI vocabularies. Reproducible SQL pipelines transformed de-identified data into OMOP CDM version 5.4 within a PostgreSQL environment. Core standardized tables included PERSON, VISIT_OCCURRENCE, CONDITION_OCCURRENCE, MEASUREMENT, OBSERVATION, DRUG_EXPOSURE, and CONDITION_ERA. Data quality was evaluated using the OHDSI Data Quality Dashboard across plausibility, conformance, and completeness domains, followed by iterative correction of mapping, date, vocabulary, and domain-related issues.
RESULTS: More than 6,300 patient records were standardized, including 2,159 respiratory disease records, 2,427 tuberculosis records, and approximately 1,800 HIV records. Data Quality Dashboard pass rates ranged from 98% to 99% across the implemented clinical domains. For the HIV CDM, 934 of 950 applicable and executable checks passed, corresponding to a corrected pass rate of 98%. HIV data achieved pass rates of 99% for plausibility, 97% for conformance, and 97% for completeness. The standardized ecosystem enabled reusable cohort definitions, cross-programme analyses, automated data-quality assessment, and the preparation of analysis-ready datasets for machine-learning applications. Major challenges included French-language and free-text terminology, inconsistent date formats, incomplete source metadata, empty source fields, and limited local expertise in clinical vocabulary mapping. These challenges were addressed through multidisciplinary clinical review, standardized mapping rules, version-controlled ETL scripts, and repeated quality-assurance cycles.
CONCLUSION: This implementation demonstrates that a tertiary hospital in a resource-constrained African setting can establish a high-quality, interoperable, and AI-ready clinical data foundation using open standards and locally led technical capacity. OMOP CDM does not constitute an artificial intelligence model itself; rather, it provides the standardized and governed infrastructure required for reproducible AI development, validation, and future federated research. The Douala experience provides a practical model for expanding interoperable hospital data pipelines across Cameroon while preserving local data ownership and strengthening national readiness for responsible AI adoption in health.

title: Blockchain as a Service (BCaaS) for Healthtech & MedTech
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study was conducted / ideated as Healthtech & MedTech domain is undergoing a major shift towards Health records and data management. There is a vital need of a universal patient record in a distributed ledger and new approaches to ensure collaborative health when we can manage our own wellness outside of the system are required to improve surgical outcome, contain healthcare costs. title: The ACE Framework: Strengthening Data Ecosystems and Interoperability for Evidence-Informed Maternal and Newborn Health Decision-Making in Nigeria
abstract:
Introduction: Nigeria has made substantial investments in digital health infrastructure, including the National Health Management Information System (NHMIS), District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2), Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR), electronic medical records, and community-based reporting systems. Despite increased data availability, maternal and newborn mortality remains high. A key challenge is not the generation of health data but fragmented information systems, limited interoperability, and inadequate use of routine data to inform planning and service delivery. This paper presents the Analyse-Convene-Execute (ACE) Framework as a practical approach to strengthening data ecosystems and institutionalizing evidence-informed decision-making for maternal and newborn health in Nigeria.
Methods: A policy and implementation analysis was conducted using a synthesis of published evidence on Nigeria's maternal and newborn health information systems and implementation experiences shared during a multi-stakeholder webinar convened by ACE Group. Evidence from policymakers, programme implementers, digital health experts, and frontline health workers was examined to identify barriers to effective data use and opportunities for strengthening health information systems. Findings informed the development of the ACE Framework.
Results: The analysis identified four major barriers to effective use of routine health data: fragmented and poorly interoperable information systems, a reporting culture focused on compliance rather than decision-making, limited analytical capacity and decision-support tools at the facility level, and centralized governance that constrains timely local action. Implementation experiences demonstrated that integrating community-generated data with routine facility information, strengthening leadership commitment, institutionalizing multidisciplinary data review platforms, and empowering local managers improve the translation of evidence into action. The resulting Analyse-Convene-Execute (ACE) Framework comprises three interconnected pillars: Analyse, which promotes the routine integration and analysis of data from multiple health information systems to generate actionable insights; Convene, which institutionalizes multidisciplinary data review and collaborative decision-making across all levels of the health system; and Execute, which empowers health managers to translate evidence into timely operational, clinical, and managerial actions through decentralized decision-making and continuous quality improvement. These pillars are underpinned by continuous learning and accountability, creating an iterative cycle that transforms routine health information into improved planning, resource allocation, service delivery, and health system performance.
Conclusion: Improving maternal and newborn health outcomes requires a shift from data collection to routine data use. The ACE Framework provides a practical approach for strengthening data ecosystems, improving interoperability, and institutionalizing evidence-informed decision-making within Nigeria's health system. Embedding this framework into national and subnational health programmes has the potential to improve governance, resource allocation, service quality, and accountability while supporting more integrated and resilient digital health systems.

title: VitalID: An AI-Enabled Digital Health Identity Platform for Improving Emergency Healthcare Delivery in Nigeria
abstract:
Background: Fragmented medical records are a persistent barrier to safe, timely care in Nigeria's health system. When patients transfer between facilities, critical clinical information is frequently lost or inaccessible, increasing the risk of diagnostic delay and medical error, particularly in emergency and maternal-referral settings.
Problem Validation: A 2025 report by The Punch found that over 60% of emergency patients presenting at Nigerian public hospitals arrive without transferable medical records. WHO data attribute nearly 30% of global maternal deaths in 2023 to Nigeria, with missing antenatal histories and poor inter-facility communication identified as contributing factors.
Proposed Solution: VitalID is an AI-enabled digital health identity platform that issues each user a unique, verifiable health ID linked to their medical history. A low-cost NFC/QR credential, HealthTag, allows authorized providers to retrieve critical patient data at the point of care. An integrated AI layer generates concise clinical summaries, flags allergies and chronic conditions, and produces emergency risk alerts to support rapid decision-making. SMS/USSD access ensures functionality in low-connectivity environments, addressing infrastructure constraints common across the health system.
Methodology: A prototype will be developed and tested through simulated emergency scenarios, evaluating record-retrieval speed, data accuracy, and provider usability against baseline (paper-based/no-record) workflows.
Expected Impact: VitalID is designed to improve continuity of care, strengthen interoperability across facilities, and reduce emergency treatment delays, contributing to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure).

title: BUILDING INTEROPERABLE FACILITY-REFERRAL AND PATIENT-RECORD INFRASTRUCTURE AS THE DATA FOUNDATION FOR AI-ENABLED HEALTH SYSTEMS IN NIGERIA
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognised as a transformative tool for strengthening health systems; however, its effectiveness depends on the availability of high-quality, interoperable health data. In Nigeria, referral pathway linking primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of care, remains fragmented with patient records are similarly distributed across disconnected facilities and digital platforms with limited interoperability, restricting longitudinal care, health information exchange, and advanced analytics. Across Africa, fragmented data ecosystems, limited interoperability, uneven digital connectivity, and gaps in data governance represent important constraints to the effective and sustainable adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in health systems. This study synthesises the evidence linking referral-system fragmentation and health-data interoperability to AI readiness in Nigerian and African health systems.
METHODS: A narrative synthesis was undertaken using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Searches combined terms across three domains: (1) referral systems, referral effectiveness, and continuity of care in Nigeria and Africa; (2) electronic health records, health-information systems, and interoperability in Nigeria; and (3) AI readiness, digital infrastructure, health-data governance, and AI implementation in African health systems. Peer-reviewed literature directly relevant to these domains was prioritised, supplemented by authoritative reports and policy documents from international and national health agencies. Titles, abstracts, and articles were screened based on predefined inclusion criteria, and 30 out of 107 identified literatures met eligibility for final review. The evidence was thematically synthesised to identify recurring structural barriers, their interrelationships, and their implications for digital health and AI-enabled care.
RESULTS: Three interrelated themes emerged, namely (1) Referral processes were commonly characterised by incomplete documentation, weak bidirectional communication, and limited feedback between levels of care, resulting in fragmented rather than continuous care pathways, (2) The coexistence of aggregate reporting platforms such as DHIS2 with fragmented patient-level records limits the availability and exchange of longitudinal data required for coordinated clinical care, secondary use, and advanced analytics, (3) Evidence from African digital-health and AI-readiness assessments consistently identifies enabling infrastructure, including data quality, interoperability, connectivity, governance, workforce capacity, and institutional readiness, as critical determinants of whether AI applications can be implemented, evaluated, and sustained. This framework is being operationalized through the ongoing development of "myfigohealth" by Otabel, an interoperability-first digital health platform designed to connect all levels of care i.e. primary, secondary, and tertiary thereby strengthening referral system, ensuring continuity of care, and establishing AI-ready health data ecosystem.
CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that limitations in underlying health-data ecosystems may constrain AI value independently of advances in algorithmic capability. However, the potential of AI to strengthen Nigerian health systems is contingent on the availability of reliable, interoperable, patient-linked health information and the institutional capacity to govern and use such data. Strengthening referral documentation and feedback mechanisms, improving interoperability across facility-level information systems, and adopting open standards such as HL7 FHIR should therefore be treated as foundational components of responsible AI readiness. Therefore, by positioning interoperability as the enabling layer between existing health information systems and future AI applications, this work provides a practical roadmap for digital health transformation in Nigeria and similar low- and middle-income settings.

title: Strengthening Financial Governance and Fiduciary Accountability through the PHC Financial Management System (PHC-FMS) under Nigeria’s Basic Health Care Provision Fund
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Primary health care (PHC) is the foundation of Nigeria's health system and the primary platform for delivering essential health services. Established under the National Health Act, the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) was designed to strengthen PHC financing by expanding fiscal space, supporting the Basic Minimum Package of Health Services (BMPHS), financing routine facility operations, and improving equitable access to care, particularly for underserved populations. However, BHCPF financial management relied largely on paper-based processes. Facility business plans, expenditure reports, and supporting documents were manually prepared and transmitted across multiple administrative levels for review and approval. These fragmented processes contributed to reporting delays, limited visibility into fund utilisation, reduced transparency, and constrained timely and accountable stewardship of public resources.
METHODS: To address these challenges, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), in collaboration with Isuna Technologies, designed and implemented the first-of-its-kind Primary Health Care Financial Management System (PHC-FMS), an integrated web- and mobile-based platform for managing BHCPF-related financial processes. The platform enables the electronic preparation and submission of quarterly business plans, real-time recording of facility income and expenditures, standardised financial documentation, automated multi-level review and approval workflows, and interactive dashboards for monitoring and oversight. Following pilot implementation in six states, iterative feedback from users and stakeholders informed system refinements ahead of phased expansion to 21 states. The roll-out was supported by targeted capacity-building for facility managers and relevant government stakeholders.
RESULTS: PHC-FMS transitioned participating facilities from paper-based to digital financial management, improving the efficiency and standardisation of financial reporting. Following phased scale-up, the platform has been deployed across 21 states, supporting 4,975 primary healthcare facilities in 452 Local Government Areas. A total of 4,975 Facility Officers-in-Charge (OICs) and more than 1,356 LGA-level users have been trained to support implementation. To date, 4,415 electronic business plans have been completed through the platform, while financial reporting has generated 81,440 income and expenditure transactions (33,031 income and 48,409 expenditure entries) from 3,519 reporting facilities. Electronic submission and approval workflows have reduced administrative bottlenecks, while real-time transaction visibility has strengthened oversight at local, state, and national levels. The platform improved the availability of timely financial data for decision-making, strengthened transparency and accountability in BHCPF fund management, and enhanced the capacity of oversight institutions to monitor resource utilisation across participating PHCs.
CONCLUSION: PHC-FMS demonstrates the potential of digital financial management systems to strengthen financial governance and fiduciary accountability within primary health care systems in resource-constrained settings. By improving the timeliness, transparency, and standardisation of financial processes, the platform supports more effective implementation of the BHCPF and contributes to stronger health system stewardship. Importantly, PHC-FMS generates timely, granular financial data that can support advanced analytics and future predictive applications, including forecasting facility funding needs and identifying potential disbursement irregularities. Continued scale-up, sustained user capacity-building, rigorous evaluation of implementation outcomes, and integration with broader national digital health architecture will be important to maximising the platform's contribution to resilient PHC systems and progress toward universal health coverage.

title: Bridging The Gap Between Awareness and Adoption: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Readiness Among Healthcare Professionals in Nigeria to Inform AI-Enabled Health System Strengthening
abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a strategic enabler of stronger, more efficient, and resilient health systems. However, successful implementation depends on a health workforce that is prepared to adopt and integrate AI into clinical practice. In Nigeria, evidence describing healthcare professionals' readiness for AI remains fragmented, limiting informed policy and implementation decisions.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guideline. Peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and May 2026 involving licensed healthcare professionals in Nigeria were identified through systematic searches of PubMed, Semantic Scholar, and Google Scholar. Data were extracted and synthesized using descriptive and thematic approaches.
Results: Forty-one studies met the inclusion criteria. Healthcare professionals consistently demonstrated high awareness and generally positive perceptions of AI, with several studies reporting awareness levels exceeding 80%. However, routine utilization remained substantially lower, frequently below 30%, demonstrating a persistent gap between awareness and implementation. Common barriers included inadequate digital infrastructure, limited AI training, implementation costs, fragmented electronic health record systems, and uncertainty surrounding governance and regulatory frameworks. Despite these constraints, healthcare professionals expressed strong willingness to acquire AI competencies and recognized AI's potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision making, and health service efficiency. Evidence was concentrated in tertiary healthcare facilities, while primary healthcare and rural settings remained underrepresented.
Conclusion: Healthcare professionals in Nigeria appear increasingly receptive to AI, yet implementation readiness remains constrained by systemic workforce, infrastructure, and governance challenges. Strengthening workforce capacity, digital infrastructure, implementation research, and national AI governance frameworks will be critical for translating awareness into sustainable AI adoption and strengthening resilient health systems across Africa.
