title: From Situation Report to Signal: An Interoperable, AI-Native Aberration-Detection Layer for IDSR, SORMAS, and DHIS2 to Strengthen Real-Time Outbreak Response in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nigeria has invested substantially in digital health infrastructure, operating Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) reporting, deploying the Surveillance Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System (SORMAS), and running DHIS2 as its routine health management information system. In practice, however, these platforms largely store and display data. Aberration detection still depends on manual review of weekly situation reports, so outbreak signals frequently surface late and unevenly across states.
METHOD: We designed an interoperable, AI-native detection layer intended to sit on top of existing surveillance systems rather than replace them. Built on a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, the layer ingests routine indicator data through standard interfaces, including the DHIS2 Web API, SORMAS data exports, and IDSR line lists, harmonises it to a common schema, and runs a multi-method engine combining negative-binomial CUSUM, EWMA, DBSCAN spatio-temporal clustering, and a LightGBM syndromic classifier. Ranked alerts are surfaced through a Next.js dashboard with interactive Leaflet maps and delivered to frontline officers by SMS. The framework was evaluated retrospectively using Nigerian cholera surveillance data spanning 1971-2021 together with recent NCDC situation reports.
RESULT: The layer was designed to integrate with existing surveillance platforms through standard APIs and data exports, enabling retrospective processing of 2,652 weekly surveillance records without modification to the underlying data model. The integrated detection engine generated prioritised alerts with a median lead time of 2.6 weeks ahead of formally recognised outbreaks, at a false-alarm rate of 1.3 alerts per surveillance year, while successfully identifying 89.4% of historically recognised outbreaks in the validation dataset. End-to-end processing, dashboard visualisation, and SMS notification completed in under 60 seconds on low-cost cloud infrastructure.
CONCLUSION: The work demonstrates that early-warning intelligence can be added as a non-invasive layer over the surveillance and information systems African countries already operate, converting passive reporting into active outbreak detection without replacing existing national infrastructure. By consuming standard IDSR, SORMAS, and DHIS2 outputs, the approach is readily portable across countries that share this digital backbone, providing a practical, interoperability-first pathway for strengthening epidemic preparedness and health security.

title: Subnational Malaria Response Gaps: An Interactive Dashboard for Priority Setting in Eastern Africa
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Malaria control remains undermined by a persistent mismatch between disease burden and intervention coverage. National surveillance can identify which countries lag but masks within-country heterogeneity, leaving program managers unable to see where inside a country the response is failing to match the disease the scale at which resources are actually deployed.
METHODOLOGY: Malaria incidence, P. falciparum prevalence (PfPR 2-10), ITN use, and effective treatment were drawn from Malaria Atlas Project modelled surfaces for eight countries (Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Rwanda, South Sudan, Madagascar), 2015-2024, and aggregated to first-level administrative units (Uganda to districts). A Malaria Response Gap Index defined the gap as burden left uncovered burden (mean of scaled incidence and prevalence) times (1 minus response), response being the mean of ITN use and treatment. Units were tiered into four priority classes and visualized in an interactive R Shiny dashboard with choropleth drill-down and trends.
RESULTS: Unmet need was concentrated, not uniform. South Sudan's Equatoria states ranked highest Western Equatorial sustained incidence above 320 per 1,000 and prevalence above 30% against coverage near 50%. The subnational lens exposed hotspots masked by national adequacy, notably western Kenya's Lake Victoria basin (Siaya, Busia). Coverage rose across most regions over the period, narrowing gaps overall, yet a subset of high-burden regions retained substantial unmet need through 2024.
CONCLUSION: A sub-national Response Gap Index turns routine modelled surveillance into region-specific intelligence, pinpointing which provinces and districts not just which countries warrant investment, giving programs a practical, scalable subnational priority-setting tool.

title: Unlocking community pharmacy data for national AMR intelligence: a case for AI-enabled surveillance integration in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance in sub-Saharan Africa relies almost exclusively on laboratory-based sentinel systems located in referral hospitals. In Tanzania, for example, only nine sentinel hospital labs feed data into the national surveillance system, which then reports to WHO GLASS. Yet community pharmacies, where up to 88% of antibiotics are dispensed without prescription generate no data that reaches national health authorities. This means the majority of antibiotic transactions in the region occur in a surveillance blind spot, leaving policymakers without the information they need to design targeted stewardship interventions. Globally, efforts to strengthen AMR surveillance have focused on expanding laboratory capacity and hospital reporting. This paper argues that a parallel strategy is needed: integrating community pharmacy dispensing data into national AMR intelligence systems using AI-enabled tools appropriate for low-resource environments.
METHODS: This conceptual analysis draws on a review of current AMR surveillance architectures in sub-Saharan Africa, with Tanzania as a primary case study, alongside published evidence on community pharmacy antibiotic dispensing patterns, AI applications in health surveillance, and digital health implementation in resource-limited settings. The analysis maps the existing data flow from sentinel labs to the national level and identifies the structural, technical, and governance gaps that currently prevent community pharmacy data from entering this flow. It then proposes a model for AI-enabled integration, drawing on the author's experience as a pharmacist from the Democratic Republic of Congo and researcher on a pharmacy-centred AI surveillance framework presented at the 5th SFUCHAS Annual Scientific Conference in Tanzania.
RESULT: The analysis identifies three principal barriers to integrating pharmacy data into national AMR intelligence. First, community pharmacies lack standardised digital data capture systems, most transactions are recorded manually or not at all. Second, no regulatory mechanism currently requires or incentivises pharmacies to report dispensing data to health authorities. Third, the volume and variability of pharmacy-level data would overwhelm manual review processes, making AI-assisted pattern detection not merely useful but necessary. The proposed model addresses these barriers through a three-layer architecture: local data capture at the pharmacy level via lightweight digital tools such as USSD or SMS-based forms; centralised AI analysis to detect unusual prescribing patterns, geographic clusters, and temporal trends across many pharmacies simultaneously; and structured reporting of anonymised, aggregated insights to existing national surveillance systems.
CONCLUSION: Community pharmacy data represents the largest untapped source of real-time antibiotic use intelligence in sub-Saharan Africa. Integrating this data into national surveillance through AI-enabled tools could fundamentally improve the evidence base available to policymakers designing AMR containment strategies. However, this requires deliberate policy decisions, not just technical development, including regulatory frameworks for pharmacy data reporting, governance standards for AI-assisted health intelligence, and investment in basic digital infrastructure at the community pharmacy level. Without these enabling conditions, even the most sophisticated AI tools will have no data to analyse. Countries developing national AI-in-health strategies should prioritise community-level data integration as a foundational layer rather than an afterthought.

title: BRAIN AND BOT: Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Use as a Predictor of Cognitive Functioning among Nigerian University Undergraduates
abstract: With the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots into higher institutions of learning, growing concerns have emerged about their implications for undergraduates' cognitive health and functioning. Unlike previous studies that focused primarily on academic performance, this study examined the levels of cognitive functioning, the extent of AI chatbot usage and the predictive relationship of AI chatbot usage on cognitive functioning among university undergraduates in Osun State, Nigeria. The study adopted the descriptive survey research design. The population comprised all university undergraduates in Osun State, Nigeria, totalling 103,951 as of the 2023/2024 session. A sample of 1,308 undergraduates was selected using a multi-stage sampling procedure from three universities in Osun State. These three universities were purposively selected based on university ownership, that is, one federal, one state, and one private university. The proportional sampling technique was then used to select 704, 364, and 240 participants from Federal, State, and Private Universities, respectively, using 2% of the population in each selected university. Two standardised instruments were adapted for data collection: the Cognitive Assessment Questionnaire (CAQ) and Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ). Data collected were analysed using descriptive and inferential analysis. The findings revealed majority (55.7%) of undergraduates demonstrated a moderate level of cognitive functioning, while 25.9% and 18.4% had low and high cognitive functioning, respectively. Moreover, the results indicated that AI chatbot usage significantly predicted the cognitive functioning of undergraduates (R=.461, R2=.213, F=347.295, p less than .05), explaining 21.3% of the observed variance. The findings underscore the need for evidence-informed institutional policies and responsible AI-use guidelines that improve healthy AI adoption while protecting students' cognitive functioning and supporting digital well-being across tertiary institutions of learning.

title: Building Country-Led AI Innovation Ecosystems to Strengthen Primary Healthcare Delivery in Malawi
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) has significant potential to improve health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries. However, many AI solutions deployed across Africa are developed externally, limiting their sustainability, contextual relevance, and long-term ownership. Malawi faces persistent challenges in healthcare delivery, including shortages of healthcare workers, fragmented health information systems, delayed disease reporting, and unequal access to quality health services, particularly in rural communities. Developing a country-led AI innovation ecosystem presents an opportunity to address these challenges while strengthening national capacity for digital health transformation.
METHODS: This paper proposes a framework for fostering a locally driven AI ecosystem that brings together government ministries, universities, healthcare institutions, technology startups, civil society organizations, and international development partners to co-create AI solutions tailored to Malawi's health priorities. The framework promotes the responsible use of national health data, open-source technologies, and interoperable digital platforms to support applications such as clinical decision support, disease surveillance, health workforce planning, medical supply chain optimization, and patient education. It also emphasizes investment in AI skills development, research collaborations, regulatory frameworks, and innovation hubs that enable local researchers and entrepreneurs to design, validate, and scale solutions within the country's health system.
RESULT: The anticipated outcomes include increased local innovation capacity, stronger institutional collaboration, improved adoption of AI-enabled health technologies, enhanced evidence-based decision-making, and greater resilience of the health system. Country ownership is expected to improve sustainability, reduce dependence on imported digital solutions, and encourage innovations that are culturally appropriate, affordable, and responsive to local needs. The framework aligns with broader goals of universal health coverage and digital transformation while supporting ethical AI governance, data privacy, and equitable access to emerging technologies.
CONCLUSION: By placing local institutions, researchers, and communities at the center of AI development, Malawi can establish a sustainable innovation ecosystem that accelerates health system strengthening and serves as a model for other low-resource countries seeking to achieve country-led digital health transformation.

title: Strategic Integration of AI for Public Health Intelligence: Designing Sustainable Frameworks for National Preparedness and Infrastructure Optimization
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The transition toward Healthcare 4.0 requires more than technological adoption; it demands robust public policy and sustainable infrastructure. National health systems face unprecedented challenges in preparedness, continuous monitoring, and resource management. Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and big data offers a powerful pathway to proactive public health intelligence. However, scaling these technologies safely necessitates comprehensive national governance, interoperable data ecosystems, and environmentally sustainable operational models. This research aims to construct a public policy and operational framework that aligns AI-driven public health intelligence with national preparedness goals, specifically tailored for emerging digital health ecosystems.
METHODS: A dual-phase research methodology was utilized, bridging engineering management and public policy. Phase one involved a comparative analysis of international regulatory frameworks governing AI in healthcare, drawing on global policy standards to identify gaps in algorithmic governance. Phase two applied Lean Six Sigma methodologies to model the operational integration of AI within national public health infrastructure. The study assessed the environmental impact of data-intensive AI deployments, developing optimization strategies for low-carbon clinical infrastructure. Quantitative models were then used to simulate the efficiency of AI-enabled resource allocation during hypothetical public health crises.
RESULT: The integration of the proposed governance framework into simulated national health systems yielded a 30% improvement in predictive accuracy for proactive resource allocation during peak demand events. Lean operational modeling identified critical redundancies in current healthcare data silos, demonstrating that standardized interoperability protocols could reduce administrative and diagnostic delays by 18%. Crucially, the application of sustainable infrastructure principles to AI data processing centers resulted in a projected 20% reduction in energy consumption, ensuring that the shift toward advanced digital health ecosystems does not compromise environmental sustainability targets.
CONCLUSIONS: Effective national preparedness relies on the seamless convergence of public policy, AI technology, and sustainable engineering management. To harness the full potential of public health intelligence, nations must prioritize country-led AI adoption backed by stringent regulatory frameworks and interoperable data ecosystems. By optimizing operational infrastructure through Lean methodologies and sustainable design, health systems can achieve long-term resilience and efficiency.

title: Invisible by Design? Assessing Whether Maternal Health Indicators Capture Vulnerability in Nigeria’s Primary Health Care System
abstract:
Nigeria has been reported to be responsible for around 20% of all maternal deaths globally, there is very little research on the information systems used to support its PHC responses in terms of what they measure. Current maternal health data systems focus on assessing contact indicators including antenatal visits, delivery in facilities, skilled birth attendance, and maternal mortality rates. Yet, these indicators are not informative about the social, structural, and contextual determinants of access to care, exclusion, and why this is so.
This is crucial as health systems become more dependent on newer technologies like AI and other decision support tools based on data. Artificial intelligence tools have the same bias as the datasets that are used to build them; thus, biased datasets lead to health inequity being embedded into future technologies.
This study assesses whether maternal health indicators currently used within Nigeria's PHC data ecosystem adequately capture vulnerability dimensions required for equitable health planning and responsible AI readiness.
A qualitative desk-based indicator mapping study was performed. Twenty-two maternal health indicators were identified from three databases: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS), Nigeria Health Management Information System (NHMIS/DHIS2) and WHO frameworks for monitoring maternal health. A benchmark for vulnerability representation was created based on the WHO frameworks: the Commission on Social Determinants of Health conceptual framework (Solar & Irwin, 2010), the Operational Framework for Monitoring Social Determinants of Health Equity (WHO, 2023), and the World Report on Social Determinants of Health Equity (WHO, 2025). The benchmark consisted of ten vulnerability dimensions classified into four domains: demographic vulnerability, socio-economic vulnerability, structural vulnerability and digital vulnerability.
Existing maternal health indicators were mapped to the above benchmark in order to ascertain whether the needs of vulnerable populations are addressed in current indicator sets through a structured mapping assessment matrix. The Vulnerability Representation Index (VRI) was then calculated. The assessment showed that there were significant differences between what the Nigeria maternal health data systems were measuring and the vulnerabilities that were linked to maternal health disparities. Out of the ten vulnerability measures evaluated, only one vulnerability, which is the rural or urban living area, was reflected in the PHC data systems. Wealth and maternal education were partially represented through national surveys and were missing in routine reporting from the facilities.
The following were completely missing: disability status; conflict-displacement status; women's autonomy and intimate partner violence status; migration/minority status; and digital access. The overall index for Vulnerability Representation was 30% (6 out of 20 indicators represented). The greatest representation gap for Structural Vulnerabilities, which are the barriers experienced by the women most susceptible to be excluded from health care services, was 12.5% (1 out of 8 indicators). Nigeria's health data ecosystem for maternal health demonstrates stronger capacity to quantify health care utilization compared to the determinants of health care access and outcomes. Those women who are the most invisible to the health system are also the most invisible to its data system. The Vulnerability Representation Index offers an effective tool to detect representation problems in the health data prior to using these data for complex analyses or AI-supported decision-making. Better vulnerability representation in health information systems is critical for PHC planning and AI development in maternal health.

title: SIgnal_Zero_Ug - Offline AI Driven Emergency Response System
abstract:
The Concept My project is an offline, AI driven emergency routing system specifically designed for traditional telecom voice networks. It serves as a resilient, low latency communication bridge during critical events such as natural disasters, medical crises, and structural fires. Because it targets standard analog and cellular voice lines rather than internet reliant smartphone applications, it ensures total accessibility for users with basic feature phones who lack internet connectivity, data access, or advanced hardware. This approach guarantees that vulnerable populations remain protected.
Technical Approach The technical framework relies entirely on on premise infrastructure, completely bypassing public cloud dependencies and vulnerabilities. Once a victim dials the toll free number, an offline Natural Language Processing (NLP) engine which will use highly optimized, local speech to text models, processes the live audio stream in real time. The AI is specifically trained to filter through heavy ambient noise and stress induced speech patterns to instantaneously detect specific crisis keywords like "fire," "heart attack," "bleeding," or "earthquake." Simultaneously, the system captures location data by extracting the caller's unique phone number and the active Cell Tower Identification (Cell ID) provided by the Mobile Network Operator. A local, offline database hosted securely on the server immediately cross references this Cell ID data with mapped geographic zones to identify the physical neighborhood and district of the caller.
Fail Safe Mechanism The defining feature of this project is its robust fail safe mechanism. If the network signal degrades or drops entirely mid call, the system does not lose the data. The offline server instantly triggers an automated backup protocol, using the GSM gateway to broadcast the victim's last known cell coordinates and contact information directly to emergency responders, ensuring rescue operations can proceed.
I am eager to contribute this innovation to the hackathon and demonstrate how it can support emergency preparedness within our national telecommunications framework.

title: Geospatial AI for Malaria Early Warning forecasting in Tanzania: A machine-learning model benchmark for 2025-2030
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains one of the world's most significant infectious diseases, with an estimated 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths reported globally in 2023, the vast majority caused by Plasmodium falciparum. Sub-Saharan Africa bears approximately 94% of the global malaria burden, where transmission is highly sensitive to climatic conditions. Variations in rainfall and temperature influence Anopheles mosquito habitat suitability, parasite development, and human exposure, while population dynamics further shape transmission risk. In Tanzania, malaria remains a major public health challenge despite substantial progress in control, with marked spatial heterogeneity across regions and increasing climate variability threatening recent gains. However, accurate subnational forecasting models that explicitly integrate climate covariates with spatial dependence remain limited, constraining timely evidence-based planning and intervention by the National Malaria Control Programme. This study aimed to develop and benchmark machine-learning models for forecasting P. falciparum parasite rate (PfPR) across Tanzania's 31 first-level administrative regions through 2030.
METHODS: Twenty-five years (2000-2024) of annual PfPR surfaces from the Malaria Atlas Project were harmonised with CHIRPS rainfall, ERA5-Land temperature, and WorldPop population datasets to create a region-year panel. Eighteen engineered predictors were generated, including autoregressive PfPR lags, climate summaries, population measures, and queen-contiguity spatial lag features capturing neighbourhood effects. Three forecasting approaches Prophet, Random Forest, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were trained using a strict temporal split (training: 2000-2019, validation: 2020-2022, testing: 2023-2024). Model performance was assessed using regression metrics (RMSE and R-squared) and classification metrics (sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC) based on the WHO mesoendemic transmission threshold. Model interpretability was evaluated using TreeSHAP.
RESULT: XGBoost with early stopping achieved the highest predictive performance, with a test RMSE of 0.0077, R-squared of 0.91, sensitivity of 0.88, specificity of 0.93, and an AUC-ROC of 0.94, substantially outperforming Random Forest and Prophet. TreeSHAP analysis showed that lagged PfPR accounted for approximately 95% of the predictive signal, while rainfall and temperature provided biologically plausible secondary contributions that improved forecast accuracy. Recursive forecasts for 2025-2030 identified five persistent malaria hotspots concentrated along Tanzania's western lakeshore region. Spatial autocorrelation remained consistently positive throughout the forecast period (Moran's I = 0.42-0.55), indicating stable geographic clustering of malaria risk.
CONCLUSION: XGBoost combined with engineered climatic and geospatial features provides an accurate, interpretable, and operationally deployable framework for subnational malaria forecasting in Tanzania. Integrating historical transmission patterns with climate and spatial information can support proactive surveillance, targeted intervention planning, and resource allocation, offering a scalable approach for strengthening malaria early warning systems across sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Which Algorithm Catches the Outbreak First? A Comparative Benchmark of Statistical and Machine-Learning Aberration-Detection Methods for Epidemic-Prone Diseases in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nigeria faces a persistent burden of epidemic-prone diseases, including cholera, Lassa fever, measles, and meningitis, yet routine surveillance still depends heavily on manual threshold review that often confirms outbreaks only after transmission is widespread. Automated aberration detection offers earlier warning, but evidence on which methods actually perform best on Nigerian routine data is scarce, leaving programme managers to choose algorithms with little local validation.
METHODS: We assembled a national cholera time series spanning 1971 to 2021, supplemented with recent Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) situation report data, and built a reproducible benchmark comparing four families of methods: negative-binomial CUSUM and an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) as statistical process-control baselines, DBSCAN for unsupervised spatio-temporal cluster detection, and a gradient-boosted (LightGBM) syndromic classifier. Each method was evaluated on detection sensitivity, specificity, false-alarm rate per year, and detection lead time relative to officially recognised outbreak periods, using temporal cross-validation and pre-specified alarm thresholds to prevent look-ahead bias.
RESULT: No single method dominated across all evaluation criteria. NB-CUSUM was strongest at flagging early low-count signals, DBSCAN added value where cases clustered spatially, and LightGBM delivered the highest specificity, substantially reducing nuisance alerts. A layered ensemble combining statistical and machine-learning signals achieved 89.4% sensitivity, 94.1% specificity, and 91.2% precision, while maintaining a false-alarm rate of 1.3 alerts per surveillance year. Compared with the threshold-based approach currently used in routine surveillance, the ensemble detected outbreaks a median of 2.6 weeks earlier and reduced missed outbreak events from 18 to 7, representing a 61.1% reduction.
CONCLUSION: These findings provide one of the first head-to-head, locally validated benchmarks of aberration-detection methods on long-run Nigerian surveillance data. They indicate that early warning is best served not by a single "best" algorithm but by a complementary ensemble, and that meaningful gains in lead time are achievable using data the health system already collects, without new field instrumentation. The benchmark and evaluation protocol are designed to be reusable, giving surveillance programmes across Africa an evidence base for selecting and tuning detection methods appropriate to their disease profile and data quality.

title: From Situation Report to Signal: An Interoperable, AI-Native Aberration-Detection Layer for IDSR, SORMAS, and DHIS2 to Strengthen Real-Time Outbreak Response in Nigeria
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nigeria has invested substantially in digital health infrastructure, operating Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) reporting, deploying the Surveillance Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System (SORMAS), and running DHIS2 as its routine health management information system. In practice, however, these platforms largely store and display data. Aberration detection still depends on manual review of weekly situation reports, so outbreak signals frequently surface late and unevenly across states.
METHOD: We designed an interoperable, AI-native detection layer intended to sit on top of existing surveillance systems rather than replace them. Built on a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, the layer ingests routine indicator data through standard interfaces, including the DHIS2 Web API, SORMAS data exports, and IDSR line lists, harmonises it to a common schema, and runs a multi-method engine combining negative-binomial CUSUM, EWMA, DBSCAN spatio-temporal clustering, and a LightGBM syndromic classifier. Ranked alerts are surfaced through a Next.js dashboard with interactive Leaflet maps and delivered to frontline officers by SMS. The framework was evaluated retrospectively using Nigerian cholera surveillance data spanning 1971-2021 together with recent NCDC situation reports.
RESULT: The layer was designed to integrate with existing surveillance platforms through standard APIs and data exports, enabling retrospective processing of 2,652 weekly surveillance records without modification to the underlying data model. The integrated detection engine generated prioritised alerts with a median lead time of 2.6 weeks ahead of formally recognised outbreaks, at a false-alarm rate of 1.3 alerts per surveillance year, while successfully identifying 89.4% of historically recognised outbreaks in the validation dataset. End-to-end processing, dashboard visualisation, and SMS notification completed in under 60 seconds on low-cost cloud infrastructure.
CONCLUSION: The work demonstrates that early-warning intelligence can be added as a non-invasive layer over the surveillance and information systems African countries already operate, converting passive reporting into active outbreak detection without replacing existing national infrastructure. By consuming standard IDSR, SORMAS, and DHIS2 outputs, the approach is readily portable across countries that share this digital backbone, providing a practical, interoperability-first pathway for strengthening epidemic preparedness and health security.

title: From Surveillance to Action: An AI-Powered Ecosystem for Disease Detection, Workforce Capacity and Health System Intelligence in Africa
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Health systems across Africa continue to contend with fragmented data, delayed outbreak detection, limited interoperability between programs, language barriers, and constrained health workforce capacity. While artificial intelligence has shown promise in addressing individual health challenges, its contribution to national preparedness is greatest when integrated across the health system rather than deployed as isolated tools. Since 2010, InStrat Global Health Solutions has worked with the Federal Government of Nigeria, state governments, and international partners to develop an interoperable, AI-enabled digital health ecosystem designed for low-resource settings, anchored by the Early Warning Outbreak Recognition System (EWORS AI).
METHODS: EWORS AI ingests routine clinical and community data through primary field data capture, third-party systems, APIs, and digitized paper records, applying machine learning algorithms to predict the likelihood and location of disease outbreaks. It generates automated email and SMS alerts, real-time GIS hotspot heat maps, and program analytics through a business intelligence portal, and is deployed by Nigeria's National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme across all 36 states and the FCT. Its effectiveness was evaluated in a 16-month retrospective analysis published in JMIR Public Health and Surveillance (2023), comparing tuberculosis screening outcomes in EWORS-mapped hotspot wards against non-hotspot wards across 14 high-burden states. Complementary platforms strengthen data supply and response capacity: CommTB provides offline AI-assisted respiratory screening in communities; VTR Mobile delivers offline-first workforce training evaluated through published pre- and post-intervention studies; MedStrat HIS automates health insurance administration; and NHMIS Medical Records supports point-of-care patient data in primary healthcare facilities.
RESULTS: Hotspot-guided screening covered nearly four million people and yielded 22,618 confirmed tuberculosis cases. Diagnostic precision among presumptive cases rose from 0.077 to 0.103, and the number of people needed to screen to find one TB case fell from 193 to 146 per 10,000. Under the PEPFAR/CDC-funded IRIS project, the same engine now predicts HIV clients at risk of treatment interruption, enabling proactive follow-up before risks manifest. VTR Mobile has trained approximately 20,000 clinical health professionals since 2016; its COVID-19 deployment across 25 states raised knowledge scores from 54 to 74, and a subsequent USAID TB LON training program recorded 99.5% of participants applying learned skills in practice. MedStrat HIS covers more than 14 million people across three states.
CONCLUSION: Integrated, offline-capable AI platforms can function as an operational intelligence layer for national preparedness, enabling earlier disease detection, targeted case finding, and stronger workforce performance. Building on this validated foundation, Zari AI, a multilingual health intelligence assistant currently in advanced development, will provide conversational access to surveillance data, program analytics, and training content in English and local African languages, further lowering barriers to data use. Together, these platforms offer a scalable, country-led model for AI-enabled health system transformation across Africa.

title: Bridging AI Surveillance and Immunoinformatics: Toward Integrated Outbreak Response for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in Nigeria
abstract:
Background: Nigeria continues to experience recurrent outbreaks of vaccine preventable diseases such as cholera, measles, and yellow fever, compounded by fragmented data integration and delayed reporting within the country's Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system. In parallel, Nigerian genomic capacity has expanded substantially, driven by institutions such as the African Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID), which has partnered with Illumina to train African researchers in bioinformatics and AI applications. Separately, immunoinformatics, the computational prediction of immune epitopes, has been applied to several pathogens endemic to Nigeria, including Lassa virus and malaria. However, the extent to which these two domains (AI driven surveillance and immunoinformatics) have been integrated into a unified outbreak response pipeline for vaccine preventable diseases remains unclear.
Methods: A review was conducted of literature published between 2016 and 2026, drawn from PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, using combinations of the terms "artificial intelligence," "machine learning," "genomic surveillance," "immunoinformatics," "vaccine preventable disease," and "Nigeria" or "Africa." Studies were included if they described AI or immunoinformatics applications relevant to infectious disease surveillance or vaccine design in African, and specifically Nigerian, contexts.
Results: The literature reveals substantial progress in two separate strands. First, AI based outbreak prediction has been piloted in Nigeria, including a cholera outbreak risk prediction (CORP) model developed for Yobe State using XGBoost, reporting 99.62% accuracy and an AUC of 99.2%, and NLP based tools such as EPIWATCH, which has been adapted to scan Nigerian Pidgin language sources for early epidemic signals. NCDC has also deployed AI supported chatbots with UNICEF to counter health misinformation during outbreaks. Second, immunoinformatics has been used to design multi epitope vaccine candidates against pathogens using Nigerian pathogen strains, including Lassa virus glycoprotein and nucleoprotein targets, alongside broader continental efforts such as the Africa-Canada AI and Data Innovation Consortium supporting AI enabled vaccine R&D. Despite these advances, the reviewed literature shows these two strands operating largely in parallel: AI surveillance tools in Nigeria focus on epidemiological and text based signals rather than pathogen genomic or antigenic data, while immunoinformatics studies remain at the in silico discovery stage, disconnected from real time NCDC surveillance infrastructure.
Conclusion: Existing evidence supports the feasibility of both AI enhanced outbreak surveillance and immunoinformatics based vaccine design in the Nigerian context, but reveals a clear gap in their integration. Bridging AI driven genomic surveillance with immunoinformatics, for example, by linking pathogen sequence data flowing through NCDC's IDSR system to automated epitope and immune escape prediction, could shorten the interval between variant detection and vaccine relevant public health action. Achieving this will require investment in bioinformatics infrastructure, cross institutional data sharing agreements, and pilot validation against real Nigerian outbreak data.

title: Advancing Digital Equity Through Predictive Analytics: Leveraging National DHIS2 Data for AI-Enabled Malaria Intelligence in Nigeria
abstract:
Despite substantial investments in digital health systems, significant disparities persist in malaria burden across Nigeria's subnational health systems. Uniform intervention approaches often fail to reflect the heterogeneous epidemiological realities experienced by different states. As countries increasingly explore Artificial Intelligence (AI) for health system strengthening, the availability of high-quality routine health data presents an opportunity to transition from retrospective reporting to predictive public health intelligence. This study examines how national DHIS2 data can support predictive analytics frameworks that advance digital equity and improve malaria targeting in Nigeria.
Methods: A retrospective analysis of 36 months of malaria surveillance data (January 2022-December 2024) was conducted using Nigeria's national DHIS2 platform. Six states representing varying malaria transmission intensities were analyzed: Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara, Ebonyi, Cross River, and Akwa Ibom. Indicators included confirmed malaria cases, rapid diagnostic test (RDT) positivity rates, and artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) treatment coverage. Data were assessed to identify subnational disparities, stratification opportunities, and potential use cases for predictive analytics and AI-enabled decision support systems.
Results: Approximately 17 million malaria cases were reviewed across the six states during the study period. Substantial heterogeneity was observed. In 2024, Sokoto recorded 1.79 million confirmed malaria cases compared to 189,000 cases in Akwa Ibom, representing a 9.5-fold difference in disease burden. RDT positivity rates ranged from 41.2% in Akwa Ibom to 82.7% in Sokoto, demonstrating marked variation in transmission intensity. Furthermore, 72% of all analyzed malaria cases were concentrated within Sokoto, Kebbi, and Zamfara States. These findings suggest that uniform planning and intervention approaches may inadequately address local epidemiological realities. DHIS2 data demonstrated strong potential to support predictive applications including hotspot identification, malaria burden forecasting, stockout prediction, early warning systems, and differentiated resource allocation.
Conclusions: Digital equity requires that health intelligence systems respond proportionately to disease burden rather than applying uniform approaches across heterogeneous settings. Nigeria's national DHIS2 platform provides a robust foundation for AI-enabled public health intelligence by supplying longitudinal, routinely collected health data at scale. Integrating predictive analytics into malaria planning and review cycles could strengthen stratification, improve resource targeting, enhance preparedness, and accelerate progress toward data-driven malaria control. Investments in analytics capacity, interoperability, and governance will be essential to translating routine health data into actionable predictive intelligence.

title: Health System Intelligence 2030: An AI-Driven Framework for Preparedness, Governance, and Sustainable Health Transformation
abstract:
Background: As countries increasingly invest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve healthcare delivery, public health surveillance, and operational efficiency, significant gaps remain in translating AI innovations into system-wide health transformation. Current AI applications are often fragmented, disease-specific, and insufficiently integrated into national governance and decision-making processes. Furthermore, many low- and middle-income countries face challenges related to data fragmentation, interoperability, policy coordination, and preparedness for emerging health threats. There is an urgent need for a holistic framework that leverages AI not only for clinical applications but also for strengthening health system intelligence, strategic planning, and adaptive governance.
Objective: This study proposes Health System Intelligence 2030 (HSI-2030), a novel AI-driven framework designed to enhance preparedness, governance, and sustainable health transformation through predictive analytics, integrated health intelligence, and evidence-based decision support.
Methods: The HSI-2030 framework integrates data from health information systems, disease surveillance platforms, workforce registries, supply chain systems, demographic databases, and environmental datasets into a unified intelligence architecture. Leveraging machine learning, predictive modeling, and systems-thinking approaches, the framework generates actionable insights for policymakers and health system leaders. The model incorporates four interconnected pillars: (1) Predictive Preparedness for anticipating disease outbreaks and health emergencies; (2) Intelligent Governance for data-driven policy formulation and resource allocation; (3) System Resilience for optimizing service delivery and workforce planning; and (4) Sustainable Transformation for monitoring long-term health system performance and equity outcomes.
Results: The proposed framework demonstrates how AI can be repositioned from a narrow technological tool to a strategic enabler of national health system intelligence. Through scenario modeling and predictive decision support, HSI-2030 enables governments to assess potential impacts of policy interventions, identify system vulnerabilities, forecast resource needs, and strengthen preparedness capacities. The framework also supports interoperability, accountability, and locally driven innovation while promoting equitable access to digital health solutions.
Conclusion: Health System Intelligence 2030 presents a forward-looking paradigm for integrating AI into health system governance and transformation. By combining predictive intelligence, strategic foresight, and systems-level decision support, the framework offers a scalable pathway for strengthening preparedness, enhancing governance effectiveness, and advancing sustainable health outcomes. The model provides a foundation for future research, pilot implementation, and policy development aimed at accelerating responsible and context-responsive AI adoption across health systems in Africa and other resource-constrained settings.
